evidence_items.locator: section 'Cash burn: the forward plan', paragraph 1

receipt.public_excerpt: The only historical burn figure in public reporting is the Wall Street Journal's $3.7 billion for Q1 2026, available only as summarized by a third party at the time of writing.

evidence_items.explanation: A reported Q1 2026 cash burn of $3.7 billion is far below 'tens of billions every few months'. But it is one quarter, second-hand, and unaudited.

evidence_items.locator: section 'Funding and how long it lasts', paragraph 1

receipt.public_excerpt: OpenAI closed a $122 billion round on 31 March 2026 at an $852 billion post-money valuation, according to a research page that cites the company. The Financial Times reported that, at the planned spending pace, that cash is on track to be used up by 2028.

evidence_items.explanation: A $122B round said to last until 2028 suggests planned spending averaging about $12B a quarter. That is high, but it also means OpenAI was not short of cash every few months. These are plan figures, not results.

receipt.public_excerpt: after entering into the agreement and investing $15 billion during the first quarter, it invested another $13.7 billion in the second quarter and the remaining $21.3 billion of its commitment sometime after June 30.

evidence_items.explanation: Confirms large inflows every quarter. These show money was raised, not that OpenAI needed it to cover costs.

evidence_items.locator: section 'Cash burn: the forward plan', paragraph 2

receipt.public_excerpt: OpenAI projects negative free cash flow of $278 billion from 2026 through 2030, alongside about $856 billion of spending on computing power and infrastructure.

evidence_items.explanation: A company plan showing very large future cash needs. This is relevant to the open clause 'will only need more money', but it is a projection, not an outcome.

unresolved_gaps: No reported cash burn for Q2 or Q3 2026, including compute prepayments.
The Q1 figure is second-hand and unaudited, and nothing confirms whether it captures all compute prepayments.
Whether the 2026 raises were needed to meet costs or were taken opportunistically is not documented.
The forward clause has no deadline and cannot be settled yet.
